Learning Objectives
Describe the anatomy of the ulnar nerve and potential sites of compression at the elbow.
Evaluate possible etiologies and risk factors for cubital tunnel syndrome.
Recognize characteristic symptoms, clinical examination findings, and diagnostic findings in
patients with cubital tunnel syndrome.
Summarize the nonsurgical and surgical management of cubital tunnel syndrome.

Ulnar Nerve Entrapment at the Elbow (Cubital Tunnel Syndrome)
Regional anatomy
The floor of the fibroosseous tunnel is formed by the medial collateral ligament of the elbow
and the joint capsule. It is bordered by the ulnar groove of the medial epicondyle and the
olecranon.
The roof is formed by the aponeurotic attachment of FCU heads from the medial epicondyle
of the humerus to the olecranon (ie, Osborne fascia or arcuate ligament).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Idiopathic Ulnar Neuropathy at the Cubital Tunnel
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001037

The ulnar nerve is subcutaneous at the medial epicondyle and experiences traction and
compressive forces during elbow flexion.
The volume of the cubital tunnel is greatest in extension and decreases by 50% with flexion
as the lumen of the canal changes from oval to slit-like.
Associated factors
Idiopathic cubital tunnel syndrome refers to ulnar neuropathy at the elbow without any
known cause.
Non-idiopathic causes of ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel may include the following:
cubitus varus and valgus deformity, prior elbow trauma, burns, heterotopic ossification,
space-occupying lesions (ganglion lipoma, osteochondroma), and arthritis.
Factors that may provoke cubital tunnel symptoms may include activities that involve
sustained elbow flexion, such as holding a phone to one’s ear, playing musical instruments
that involve elbow flexion, shaving oneself, brushing one’s hair, or brushing one’s teeth.
In patients with idiopathic ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel, the primary site of
compression is the fascia connecting the two heads of the FCU between the medial epicondyle
(Osborne ligament).
Other proposed sites of compression are more relevant after transposition (Figure 2).

Ulnar Nerve Entrapment at the Elbow (Cubital Tunnel Syndrome)
The ulnar nerve experiences traction and compression forces with elbow flexion. As the
elbow flexes, traction occurs with as much as 29% increase in strain.2 In addition, with
elbow flexion, the Osborne ligament stretches and tightens as the medial collateral
ligament loosens and bulges, which flattens the lumen of the cubital tunnel and
decreases its volume by as much as 50%. Consequently, intraneural pressures (reflective
of traction) increase above 70° of flexion, and extraneural pressures (reflective of
compression) increase above 100° of flexion. Intraneural and extraneural pressures are
lowest between 40° and 50° of flexion.3

Differentiation of idiopathic ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel (no known cause)
from discrete pathology associated with ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel is
important. This differentiation is readily evident in some patients, such as those with
ulnar neuropathy coincident with primary or posttraumatic elbow arthritis. The
distinction merits greater attention and more careful discernment in other patients. For
example, ulnar neuropathy often is falsely ascribed to intraoperative positioning of the
arm in patients in whom physical examination typically reveals marked first dorsal
interosseous atrophy, which clearly is not new.4 Evidence shows that long-standing
disease often is misperceived as new at the time symptoms are first noticed.5,6 Evidence
also shows that more than 50% of patients have weakness or atrophy of the first dorsal
interosseous muscle at the time of initial diagnosis of cubital tunnel syndrome.7
Considerations of causation merit critical assessment. Given the base rate of idiopathic
ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel, the fact that individuals may be unaware of such
neuropathy for years, the likely structural and genetic components of such neuropathy,
the safest option is to assume no association exists between an activity tied to the onset
of symptoms and the pathophysiology.
In the distal third of the arm, the ulnar nerve traverses the medial intramuscular septum
from the anterior to the posterior compartment of the arm.8 In the posterior
compartment, the ulnar nerve runs beneath a musculoaponeurotic extension from the
triceps to the medial intramuscular septum. If the ulnar nerve is transposed to a position
anterior to the medial epicondyle, it may be tethered at this site and may be subject to
compression or kinking. Opening this fascia to the point at which the ulnar nerve passes
through the medial intramuscular septum is relatively easy. Some surgeons suggest that
this technique helps limit a new point of compression after the nerve has been
transposed. The same is true with regard to the flexor-pronator aponeurosis distally
(which some describe as the distal part of the Osborne ligament).9 This anatomy likely is
less important if the nerve is released in situ (Resource 2).
The situation is similar for the medial intramuscular septum near the medial epicondyle.
If this septum is not released at the time of transposition, then the transposed nerve
may theoretically be kinked or compressed as it passes over this often taut structure.

As the nerve travels between the olecranon and the medial epicondyle, it enters the
cubital tunnel. The roof of the cubital tunnel is the key site of compression. This
structure, called the Osborne ligament, is a transverse connection between the humeral
and ulnar heads of the FCU. It is relatively thick between the medial epicondyle and the
olecranon and is thinner distally
Another potential site of compression is the anconeus epitrochlearis, a muscular
variation of the Osborne ligament that may be present in as many as 34% of
individuals.10 Experimental evidence is insufficient to determine if the presence of this
muscle increases the risk of idiopathic ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel.
Diagnosis
Altered sensation, specifically paresthesias and, if advanced, diminished sensibility in the ulnar
nerve distribution. Involvement of the dorsum of the hand may aid in differentiation from the
much less common ulnar nerve compression at the Guyon canal (Video 1).
Video 1 Adams JE: Physical examination of the hand and wrist: Inspection and palpation.
Dorsum, in Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 430-441.

Paresthesias also can occur with tapping over the nerve, the so-called Tinel sign (Video 2).

With advanced compressive ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel, flexion of thumb
interphalangeal joint may be observed during attempted key pinch (Froment sign) and laxity in
hyperextension of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint during attempted key pinch (Jeanne
sign). These findings are more commonly observed with ulnar nerve laceration or palsy (Video
3).

Armstrong AD, Hubbard MC, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Care, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 430-441.
Electrodiagnostic findings
Slowing of nerve conduction velocity across the elbow, normal or mildly prolonged motor
latency, low compound muscle action potential (CMAP) and sensory nerve action potential
amplitudes
Absolute conduction velocity less than 50 m/s or relative conduction velocity decrease
greater than 10 m/s in the segment across the elbow
CMAP amplitude decrease of at least 50% between above-elbow and below-elbow
stimulation

Needle electromyography (EMG) showing denervation in the first dorsal interosseous muscle,
abductor digiti minimi, and flexor digitorum profundus; the FCU may or may not be involved.
Additional studies include the inching study (ulnar motor conduction study with recording
over the first dorsal interosseous muscle as the stimulation site is moved incrementally
across the elbow), sensory/mixed nerve sensory potential studies across the elbow, dorsal
branch sensory study, and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve sensory studies (to
differentiate medial cord/lower trunk lesions).
Differential diagnosis
C8 or T1 radiculopathy and ulnar tunnel syndrome.
Less common diagnoses that may mimic some cubital tunnel symptoms include thoracic
outlet syndrome and Pancoast tumor

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow is based on signs and symptoms that
can be confirmed via objective testing, most commonly electrodiagnostic studies or
ultrasonography.9,11 Examination can begin at the neck and proceed distally to assess
for pathology along the course of the ulnar nerve (Resource 3).
The most common initial findings are sensory changes in the ulnar nerve distribution
that worsen with sustained elbow flexion. Sensory deficits usually are detected in the
little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger. A sensory deficit also will be present over
the dorsal ulnar aspect of the hand, which is innervated by the dorsal sensory branch of
the ulnar nerve. This finding may help differentiate compression at the elbow from the
much less common compression at the Guyon canal because the dorsal sensory nerve
branches approximately 5 to 7 cm proximal to the ulnar styloid, before the Guyon canal.
Initial abnormalities may be detected via threshold sensibility testing, such as vibratory
or Semmes-Weinstein monofilament testing because initial changes affect the threshold
rather than innervation density (eg, two-point discrimination testing). However, in
practice, two-point discrimination is commonly measured.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001037

Several provocative testing maneuvers may provoke symptoms. These maneuvers
include the Tinel sign (percussion at the retrocondylar groove) and sustained elbow
flexion (elbow flexion test) with or without direct pressure over the nerve (cubital tunnel
compression test).
Patients may describe a loss of fine motor coordination (dexterity). Muscle weakness
typically is a sign of severe neuropathy. Test the strength of the first dorsal interosseous
muscle by having the patient fully radially deviate the index finger and then resist
attempts to ulnarly deviate the index finger by pushing at the proximal interphalangeal
joint. Compare the strength of the right and left hands. Muscle atrophy, which is a sign of
the most severe neuropathy, is best appreciated in the first dorsal interosseous muscle
in the first web space. As many as 40% of patients with cubital tunnel syndrome have
muscle atrophy on initial examination.7 Additional signs of severe muscular weakness or
imbalance that may be observed include the Wartenberg sign, Froment sign, and Jeanne
sign; however, these signs are not typical of idiopathic ulnar neuropathy at the cubital
tunnel and more often are observed in patients with ulnar nerve injury.
The Wartenberg sign is observed as an inability to actively adduct the little finger
because of weakness of the third palmar interosseous muscle. Instead, the little finger
will rest in an abducted position secondary to unopposed pull of the extensor digiti
quinti muscle innervated by the radial nerve.
The Froment and Jeanne signs are observed with attempted key pinch. With the Froment
sign, thumb interphalangeal joint flexion will be observed because the median
innervated flexor pollicis longus will compensate for the weakened adductor pollicis.
With the Jeanne sign, hyperextension of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint will occur
because of loss of metacarpophalangeal stabilization by the adductor.
In patients with extremely severe disease, advanced atrophy of the intrinsic musculature
in the presence of intact extrinsic flexors may result in clawing of the ring and little
fingers (Duchenne sign).
Electrodiagnostic testing can supplement the clinical examination for cubital tunnel
syndrome, especially if differentiation between neck, elbow, or wrist pathology is

unclear.12 Testing should include motor, sensory, and mixed nerve conduction studies,
with special attention paid to motor nerve conduction velocity across the elbow
(Resource 4).
Cubital tunnel syndrome is the clinical syndrome of numbness and tingling because of
involvement of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Cubital tunnel syndrome is a clinical
diagnosis based on patient history and physical examination findings. Ulnar neuropathy
at the elbow is a condition diagnosed via electrodiagnostic testing indicating measurable
pathology in the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Findings of ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
revealed via electrodiagnostic testing represent objective evidence of pathology that
corresponds with cubital tunnel syndrome. Symptoms suggestive of cubital tunnel
syndrome without electrodiagnostic evidence of ulnar neuropathy may represent mild
ulnar neuropathy; however, caution is necessary to limit the potential for misdiagnosis.
Potential mild ulnar neuropathy can be monitored over time. Patients with incidental
electrodiagnostic evidence of ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel may not have
noticed symptoms, but they often have discernable signs on physical examination that
qualify as cubital tunnel syndrome.
In assessing motor nerve conduction, CMAP is generated by muscles innervated by the
stimulated nerve. Latency is the time from nerve stimulation to generation of the CMAP
by the muscle. Conduction speeds are determined by subtracting the latency derived at
a terminal point from the latency derived at a more distal point. The nerve conduction
velocity is then determined by dividing the conduction speed by the distance between
the terminal and distal points. Because peripheral nerve entrapment results in focal
demyelination, decreased nerve conduction velocities can be expected. Diagnostic
criteria for ulnar neuropathy are absolute conduction velocity less than 50 m/s or a
relative drop in conduction velocity greater than 10 m/s across the elbow. In addition,
normal or mildly diminished motor latencies may be observed. CMAP amplitude is a
rough estimation of the number of nerve fibers activated with nerve stimulation, and a
decrease of at least 50% between above-elbow and below-elbow amplitudes may be
observed. The inching technique can be used to study the ulnar motor nerve. In this
technique, a large interval across the elbow (10 cm) is divided into smaller segments (2
cm) and tested systematically to better localize a specific site of compression.

Sensory and mixed nerve conduction studies often are abnormal and are measured in a
manner similar to that of motor studies. These nerves can be stimulated orthodromically
(distal to proximal) or antidromically (proximal to distal). For the ulnar nerve at the
elbow, antidromic responses may be easier to obtain via measuring responses in the
ring and little fingers. In addition, specific examination of the dorsal sensory branch of
the ulnar nerve may help differentiate cubital tunnel entrapment from ulnar tunnel
entrapment.
EMG studies are used to evaluate the physiologic status of muscle function by recording
the electrical activity of a muscle during voluntary contraction. An EMG study has three
components: observation of the muscle at rest, motor unit potential on minimal
voluntary contraction, and the recruitment pattern of motor unit potentials with
maximal contraction. With muscular denervation, which is observed in patients with
advanced compressive neuropathy, the muscle membrane will become unstable and
produce spontaneous discharges at rest in the form of fibrillation potential and positive
sharp waves. These discharges typically are observed 2 to 3 weeks after muscle
denervation. In addition, the degree of voluntary contraction correlates with the number
of motor action potentials produced; greater contraction produces a greater number of
action potentials. With denervation, a lower number of motor unit potentials will be
produced with muscle contraction. In patients with cubital tunnel compression,
denervation may be observed in the first dorsal interosseous muscle, abductor digiti
minimi, and the ulnar flexor digitorum profundus. The FCU may be spared. However,
because denervation processes typically occur in patients with chronic neuropathy, EMG
studies are not as useful in detecting early compression.
Management
Nonsurgical management involves splinting the elbow in 30° to 45° of flexion and/or avoiding
prolonged elbow flexion activities.
Surgical treatment is indicated for patients with static numbness or first dorsal interosseous
weakness or atrophy and patients whose night symptoms are not relieved by attempts to limit
elbow flexion.

Advanced ulnar neuropathy with atrophy likely is permanent. Patients should be prepared for
a prolonged and incomplete recovery of nerve function. Many patients misperceive the
problem as worse or recurrent after a brief period of perceived improvement. This
misperception may lead to unhelpful repeat surgical procedures.13
In situ ulnar nerve decompression
Posterior branches of the medial brachial and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves are at
risk during surgical exposure.
Open and endoscopic techniques
No difference in clinical outcome compared with anterior transposition
In situ decompression and medial epicondylectomy (Figure 3)
Risk of iatrogenic medial collateral ligament injury and valgus elbow instability
Allows some degree of anterior transposition with less dissection and less potential for the
feeling of subluxation over the epicondyle
Anterior transposition
Subcutaneous, intramuscular, submuscular
Transposition anterior to the axis of the elbow decreases tension with flexion.
The medial part of the intermuscular septum is resected to prevent kinking of the nerve
after anterior transposition.
Theoretically, circumferential dissection may compromise blood supply and affect recovery.
Therefore, some surgeons recommend protecting the superior and inferior ulnar collateral
arteries and avoiding excessive proximal ulnar nerve dissection.

Management
Nonsurgical management includes alleviation of night symptoms by limiting elbow
flexion, which can be achieved with the use of a splint in 30° to 45° of flexion, by putting
the hand in a pillow, or by wrapping the arm with a towel.14 Nonsurgical management
may be offered to patients with intermittent symptoms and no weakness or atrophy of
the first dorsal interosseous muscle.15 Patients who are satisfied with this approach are
advised to monitor symptoms because the neuropathy is expected to worsen over the
years.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Idiopathic Ulnar Neuropathy at the Cubital Tunnel
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001037
14/26

Surgical treatment is indicated in patients with pathology localized to the cubital tunnel
and static numbness or first dorsal interosseous weakness or atrophy or if night
symptoms are not relieved by attempts to limit elbow flexion.16 The most common
surgical techniques include in situ decompression, partial medial epicondylectomy, and
anterior transposition. Although the relative advantages and disadvantages of each
treatment approach are a subject of debate, the primary goal is to fully decompress the
nerve11 (Resource 5).
In situ or simple decompression involves relieving all sites of ulnar nerve compression
while leaving the nerve in place. This technique can be carried out through a small
incision along the medial aspect of the elbow (Figures 4 and 5). Posterior branches of
the medial brachial and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves often cross the field
perpendicular to the incision and can be mobilized and preserved to limit the potential
for neuroma formation. The main sites of compression, including the medial head of the
triceps fascia, the Osborne ligament, and the deep flexor pronator aponeurosis, can be
addressed. Circumferential mobilization of the nerve is avoided to preserve the
perineural blood supply and prevent hypermobility. Early range of motion is permitted.
This technique can be performed via open and endoscopic approaches, with equivalent
outcomes via either method.17 In theory, in situ decompression does not address nerve
tension or hypermobility. Four randomized controlled studies and a meta-analysis
compared in situ decompression with anterior transposition and reported no difference
in nerve conduction velocities or symptoms between the two techniques.18-22

Surgeons must interpret the published association between in situ decompression and a
higher likelihood of secondary surgery in as many as 19% of patients with caution.23
Given that many patients may have advanced and permanent neuropathy (which most
patients do not fully recognize preoperatively), postoperative dissatisfaction can be
expected. Patients may not notice the severity of the problem until after surgical
treatment. Apparent worsening often is attributed to increased frustration with
persistent symptoms from permanent nerve damage.13 If patients who undergo in situ
decompression are dissatisfied postoperatively, surgeons may be more likely to
recommend secondary surgery. This may lead to a false association between in situ

subluxating ulnar nerves may be better suited for transposition (Video 4).
Video 4 Lee D: Video. Subluxation of the Ulnar Nerve. Nashville, TN, 2021.
Medial epicondylectomy involves decompression of the ulnar nerve followed by limited
osteotomy of the medial epicondyle (<19%) to preserve the medial collateral ligament
and prevent iatrogenic elbow instability.24 Medial epicondylectomy allows the ulnar
nerve to translate anteriorly over a smoothened medial elbow to reduce the subluxation
sensation and, in theory, reduce nerve irritation. This technique may not reduce neural
strain as effectively as anterior transposition (Figure 6).
Anterior transposition involves decompression of the ular nerve followed by
transposition of the nerve anterior to the axis of the elbow. Advocates for anterior
transposition speculate that the technique addresses tension and compression forces
associated with elbow motion (Figures 7 and 8). Because circumferential dissection of
the nerve must be carried out to allow for tension-free transposition, the superior and
inferior collateral arteries are maintained with the nerve, and excessive proximal
dissection is avoided to preserve the blood supply. The nerve can be transposed
subcutaneously (superficial to the flexor-pronator origin), intramuscularly (through a
trough in the flexor-pronator origin), or submuscularly (underneath the flexor-pronator
mass; Figures 9 and 10). With transposition, a section of the intermuscular septum is
